## 4.5 Coefficient variation and pole order

The coefficient-raising identity of [Chapter 2](#technical-information/explicit-constructions) gives a second propagation argument over the generic coefficient field. Differentiating in an even sextic direction \(C\) takes a certificate for \((q,A)\) to one for \((q+1,AC)\), preserving the reduced denominator support.

Over the universal coefficient field, the direction \(\dot{F}=C\) is a derivation. It extends uniquely to every finite separable coefficient extension in characteristic zero. Applying the identity there and then the normalized trace of Chapter 1 produces a certificate over the original field. Thus an analytic choice of solutions is unnecessary, but a generic family is necessary.

Every odd monomial of degree \(6\cdot q\) is a product of an odd sextic and \(q-1\) even sextics. To prove this, let its total \(Y\)-degree be \(s\), and choose \(b\in \{1,3,5\}\) congruent to \(s\) modulo six. Select \(b Y\) factors and \(6-b X\) factors for the odd sextic; there are enough since both remaining totals are nonnegative multiples of six. Group the remaining \(Y\) factors into all-\(Y\) sextics and the remaining \(X\) factors into all-\(X\) sextics. Iterating the raising identity and taking linear combinations proves the all-positive-\(q\) assertion.

## 4.6 Quotient representations and extension obstructions

An auxiliary quotient must both have divisor-supported cohomology and reach the required representation of the covering variety. The averaging ideal of §3.1 separates these two conditions: a new correspondence can enlarge the supported image, whereas changing a residue representative within an existing quotient does not enlarge its averaging ideal.

Deformation imposes a further condition. The generic criterion of §4.4 requires a family dominating the relevant coefficient space. The following calculations determine the dimensions and cohomological images of the paired-sign and natural cubic-cover constructions, then compare the source and target dimensions of a direct Fano-extension density test.

### The transcendental part of the surface fibers

The dimension gap is explicit. Paired signs and global \(Y\)-evenness leave 74 coefficients, since for pair degrees \(2k_i\) their monomial count is
\[
\frac12\sum_{k_0+k_1+k_2=3}
\left(\prod_i(2k_i+1)+1\right)=74.
\]
The diagonal torus preserves this space and the twelve off-diagonal Fermat orbit derivatives lie outside it, so its block-linear saturation has affine dimension \(74+12=86\), against 236 for all even sextics. No construction confined to these symmetries can dominate the full coefficient space.

The fibers show what is lost geometrically. Write an arbitrary even sextic as
\[
F=\sum_{j=0}^3F_{6-2j,2j}(X,Y).
\]
Fix \(c_i=(Y_i/X_i)/(Y_0/X_0)\), with \(c_0=1\), and quotient by \(\tau\). With \(b=(Y_0/X_0)^2\), the surface over these passive parameters compactifies to
\[
\sum_{j=0}^3 b^jr^{3-j}F_{6-2j,2j}(X,cX)=0
\quad\text{in}\quad\mathbb P^2_X\times\mathbb P^1_{(b:r)}.
\]
Its bidegree is \((6,3)\). For general coefficients it is smooth, with
\[
K=\mathcal O(3,1),\qquad q=0,\qquad p_g=20.
\]
Indeed, at fixed nonzero \(c_i\) every degree-six \(X\)-monomial occurs in each coefficient of \(b^jr^{3-j}\), so the original coefficient space surjects onto the complete \((6,3)\) linear system. Bertini and adjunction apply. Paired signs replace \(X_i\) by \(u_i=X_i^2\), giving bidegree \((3,3)\) and \(p_g=2\). The additional order-three quotient of §4.2 removes the two holomorphic forms, giving \(p_g=0\). The sequence
\[
20\quad\longrightarrow\quad2\quad\longrightarrow\quad0
\]
records the dimensions of holomorphic two-forms after the successive quotients.

Even on the smooth \((3,3)\) surface, the nontrivial order-three characters remain substantial. Its Euler number is 36 and \(b_2=34\), while its free quotient has \(b_2=10\). Each nontrivial complex eigenspace therefore has dimension twelve; the characters of the holomorphic forms give Hodge dimensions \((1,10,1)\). The ten-dimensional invariant eigenspace is entirely algebraic; the other two contain holomorphic two-forms. Thus the surface-fibration theorem does not extend to a nontrivial character merely by replacing the numerator or increasing its pole order.

Without the extra diagonal symmetry, the paired cubic has coefficients of degree at most three in \(b\); its Jacobian coefficients have degrees at most twelve and eighteen. A minimal Weierstrass model with fundamental line bundle \(\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^1}(n)\) has \(\chi(\mathcal O)=n\) and canonical bundle pulled back from \(\mathcal O(n-2)\); see [Schütt–Shioda, §§6.6 and 8.2](https://arxiv.org/abs/0907.0298). The minimal degree-\((12,18)\) case has \(n=3\) and Kodaira dimension one, so the surface is not dominated by a family of rational curves with passive parameters fixed. Coprime coefficients and an exact degree-eighteen coefficient give a useful minimality criterion: they exclude nonminimality at finite places and infinity, respectively.

### The natural cubic cover and its standard representation

There is a second useful reduction for every even sextic. Let
\[
B=\mathbb P^2_X\times\mathbb P^2_Y,\qquad
(a,b,c,d)=(F_{6,0},F_{4,2},F_{2,4},F_{0,6}).
\]
Along the line \([\lambda X:\mu Y]\), the quotient \(Q=X/\tau\) has equation
\[
a+bt+ct^2+dt^3=0,\qquad t=(\mu/\lambda)^2,
\]
on the corresponding trivializations. Its discriminant is the section of \(\mathcal O_B(12,12)\)
\[
\Delta=b^2c^2-4ac^3-4b^3d-27a^2d^2+18abcd.
\]
For a general sextic, the cubic cover has monodromy \(S_3\): it is connected, and its general branch points have simple ramification. On the open \(B^\circ\) where it is étale, its rank-three permutation local system splits as
\[
\mathbb Q\oplus V_{\mathrm{std}},
\]
where \(V_{\mathrm{std}}\) is the rank-two standard representation. The weight-four part contributed by the constant summand comes from \(H^4(B)\), hence is algebraic. Up to boundary-supported classes, the primitive problem therefore requires the standard summand. The discriminant double cover carries the sign representation, and \(V_{\mathrm{std}}^{A_3}=0\). Pulling the standard local system to that cover splits it over \(\mathbb C\) into two nontrivial cubic characters; it does not make it constant.

The quotient \(Q\) itself is not uniruled. The fixed locus of \(\tau\) consists of the two smooth plane sextic curves \(X\cap\{X=0\}\) and \(X\cap\{Y=0\}\). The tangent eigenvalues there are \((1,-1,-1,-1)\), of age \(3/2\); elsewhere the action is free. Thus the quotient has terminal transverse singularities \(\frac12(1,1,1)\) and torsion canonical class. [Kollár–Larsen, Theorem 2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0701466) gives Kodaira dimension zero and nonuniruledness of a smooth projective model.

Let \(Z\) be a smooth equivariant projective model of the \(S_3\)-Galois closure. The subgroup quotients which could serve the standard representation are determined without computing their equations:

| Subgroup \(K\subset S_3\), up to conjugacy | \(\dim V_{\mathrm{std}}^K\) | Quotient |
| --- | ---: | --- |
| \(1\) | 2 | \(Z\), which dominates \(Q\) generically finitely |
| \(C_2\) | 1 | A model of \(Q\) |
| \(A_3\) | 0 | The discriminant double cover |
| \(S_3\) | 0 | The rational base \(B\) |

The first two quotients are not uniruled: uniruledness of \(Z\) would descend through its generically finite map to \(Q\). The other two have no standard invariants. Consequently no collection of uniruled intermediate quotients of this natural Galois closure can serve \(V_{\mathrm{std}}\) through the averaging ideal of §3.1. This is a restriction on that quotient strategy. As the surface-fibration theorem shows, nonuniruledness itself is compatible with divisor support.

### A dimension obstruction to the direct Fano-extension density test

Another possible source of cycles is a containing Fano variety: vary it while keeping the section fixed, find rational Hodge classes on it, and restrict their algebraic representatives. This is the strategy of [Voisin's threefold argument](https://www.numdam.org/item/ASNSP_1992_4_19_4_473_0.pdf). Its direct ordinary extension to a sextic fourfold has a dimension obstruction. A one-coordinate extension is a fivefold, whose middle cohomology has odd weight and supplies no middle \(p,p\) classes. Consider instead the two-coordinate extension

\[
X=Y\cap\{u=v=0\},\qquad Y=\{G=0\}\subset\mathbb P^7,
\]

where \(Y\) is a smooth sextic sixfold, \(G|_{u=v=0}=F\), and the involution has the original three positive and three negative eigendirections plus signs \((\epsilon_u,\epsilon_v)\). Let \(R(G)\) be its Jacobian ring. The residue identification includes the determinant character:

\[
H^{6-p,p}(Y)_{\mathrm{prim}}^\sigma
\simeq R(G)_{6(p+1)-8}^{\det\sigma},
\qquad \det\sigma=-\epsilon_u\epsilon_v.
\]

Thus an invariant \((3,3)\) class is represented by \(Q\in R_{16}^{\det\sigma}\), and its first-order Hodge condition in a fixed-section direction \(g\) is multiplication

\[
g\longmapsto Qg\in R_{22}^{\det\sigma}
\simeq H^{2,4}(Y)^\sigma.
\]

The required surjectivity is impossible by dimension. Exact monomial counts give:

| Signs on \((u,v)\) | Invariant sextic coefficients | Fixed-section directions | After pointwise-fixing coordinate changes | \(h^{2,4}(Y)^\sigma\) |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| \((+,+)\) or \((-,-)\) | 883 | 647 | at most 637 | 6503 |
| \((+,-)\) | 868 | 632 | at most 624 | 6596 |

There are 236 invariant sextic coefficients on the fixed \(\mathbb P^5\), explaining the subtraction in the third column. The equivariant projective transformations fixing that \(\mathbb P^5\) pointwise have dimension ten for equal normal signs and eight for opposite signs. They contribute trivial Hodge variation. Even the unquotiented dimensions 647 and 632 are already too small, so the conclusion does not depend on this refinement.

For reproducibility, if \(a+b=8\) are the positive and negative coordinate counts, the first numeric column is

\[
\sum_{\substack{0\le j\le6\\j\text{ even}}}
\binom{j+b-1}{b-1}\binom{6-j+a-1}{a-1}.
\]

The last column counts degree-ten monomials with each exponent at most four and polynomial character \((-1)^b\), rather than invariably taking polynomial character \(+1\). This is the determinant twist above; complex conjugation identifies the \((4,2)\) and \((2,4)\) dimensions. The equivariant Koszul formula makes these counts constant on the smooth invariant locus. The same calculation gives \(h^{5,1}(Y)^\sigma=155\) and 170, respectively. The command `python3 scripts/verify-extension-dimensions.py` reconstructs these counts by exact monomial enumeration.

Consequently this fixed-section sixfold construction cannot provide the full invariant Hodge-bundle submersion used to obtain dense rational middle Hodge classes in the Voisin argument. The dimension bound concerns that density map: it gives no obstruction to divisor support from independently supplied cycles, smaller subvariations or different ambient geometry.

# 2A. Binary sextics and torsion contacts

Cubic-square presentations of a binary sextic give a concrete example of contact geometry. Their finite parameter space is the nonzero three-torsion of a genus-two Jacobian, modulo sign. Two spanning theorems for the associated Wronskians turn these contacts into rational fields. The resulting construction is useful independently of the two-reflection support theorem: it identifies the fields and explains why their targets span.

**Example: a binary-block family.** Let

\[
F=P_0(X_0,X_1)+P_1(Y_0,Y_1)+P_2(X_2^2,Y_2^2),
\]

where \(P_0,P_1\) are binary sextics and \(P_2\) is a binary cubic over a characteristic-zero field. Suppose \(F=0\) is smooth. Separate reflection in \(X_2\) and \(Y_2\) places this family under the [two-reflection support theorem](#technical-information/weighted-threefolds), giving certificate existence at every positive pole order. It also admits the following explicit construction.

**Binary-block construction theorem.** For \(q=1,2\) and every \(Y\)-odd \(A\) of degree \(6q\), there is a rational field satisfying
\[
qv(F)=A,\qquad \operatorname{div}v=0,
\]
with the homogeneity and legal poles of Chapter 1. It is obtained from cubic-square contacts, cubic-surface lines, linear combinations and coefficient differentiation. Normalized finite trace gives a field over the original coefficient field.

Write the three binary variable blocks as \(V_{0},V_{1},V_{2}\), and let \(P_{i}\) also denote the ordinary sextic in its block. Smoothness is equivalent to squarefreeness of all three sextics. Indeed, a multiple projective root of one block gives a nonzero zero of both its partials and hence a singular point of \(F\) with the other blocks zero. Conversely, the partials of a squarefree binary form vanish simultaneously only at the origin. For the third block, squarefreeness says that the endpoint coefficients and discriminant of \(P_{2}\) are nonzero.

## 2A.1 The elementary fields behind the construction

Suppose a block admits \(P_{i}=C_{i}^{3}+r_{i}^{2}\), with \(\operatorname{deg} C_{i}=2\) and \(\operatorname{deg} r_{i}=3\). Put

\[
\begin{gathered}
J_{i}=\{C_{i},r_{i}\}=C_{i,x}r_{i,y}-C_{i,y}r_{i,x},\\
e_{i}=r_{i}(-C_{i,y}\partial _{x}+C_{i,x}\partial _y)/(2\cdot J_{i}).
\end{gathered}
\]

Direct differentiation gives \(e_{i}(C_{i})=0, e_{i}(r_{i}^{2})=r_{i}^{2}\), and \(\operatorname{div}(J_{i}e_{i})=J_{i}/2\). In the last identity, the Hamiltonian field of \(C_{i}\) has zero divergence and takes \(r_{i}\) to \(J_{i}\). Squarefreeness implies \(J_{i}\ne 0\): otherwise \(C_{i}\) and \(r_{i}\) would be algebraically dependent, so \(P_{i}\) could not be squarefree.

For a different block \(j\) let \(E_{j}\) be its Euler field and set \(e=e_{i}+E_{j}/6\) and \(D=r_{i}^{2}+P_{j}\). Then \(e(F)=e(D)=D\). If a cubic multiplier \(M\) satisfies \(e(M)=M/6\), the field

\[
\begin{gathered}
v=J_{i}M e/D
\end{gathered}
\]

is strict for \(J_{i}M\). Indeed \(\operatorname{div}(J_{i}e)=5\cdot J_{i}/6\), so \(\operatorname{div}(J_i M e)=J_i M\); differentiation of \(1/D\) cancels this divergence. Two useful choices are \(M=C_{i}L_{j}\) and \(M=L_{j}Q_{k}\), where \(L_{j}\) is linear in block \(j, Q_{k}\) is quadratic in the remaining block, and \(i,j,k\) are distinct. They supply the \(C\cdot J\)-times-linear and raw-\(J\)-times-(linear,quadratic) packets.

For two decomposed blocks \(i,j\), take \(e=e_{i}+e_{j}, D=r_{i}^{2}+r_{j}^{2}\), and \(A=J_{i}J_{j}\). The same calculation gives \(e(F)=e(D)=D\) and \(\operatorname{div}(Ae)=A\). Hence \(Ae/D\) is strict for \(A\). Multiplying it by a homogeneous degree-six first integral \(\beta \) and dividing by two gives a strict \(q=2\) field for \(\beta A\). In particular \(\beta =C_{i}C_{j}Q_{k}\) gives the \(C\cdot J\times C\cdot J\) packet.

All these numerators are polynomial after multiplication by their displayed Jacobians. Their denominators involve only two blocks, whereas smooth \(F\) has a nonzero third block, so they are coprime to \(F\). The fields can be averaged for global \(Y\)-parity and traced in their coefficient fields. Polynomial fields \(L_{j}\partial _{x}\) and \(L_{j}\partial _y\) additionally serve \(L_{j}P_{i,x},L_{j}P_{i,y}\) strictly. Thus the remaining question is exactly what the cubics \(J\) and quintics \(C\cdot J\) span as the decompositions vary.

### An elliptic differential behind the two-contact field

The product \(J_iJ_j\) also has a useful interpretation through the moving-point current of [Chapter 2, §2.8](#technical-information/explicit-constructions). Dehomogenize two binary contacts as

\[
f(r)=C(r)^3+R(r)^2,\qquad
g(s)=D(s)^3+S(s)^2,
\qquad P(t)=f(r)+g(s)t^6.
\]

On the rational open where the following denominators are nonzero, adjoin

\[
\alpha^3=iR/S,\qquad \beta^3=-P(\alpha),\qquad i^2=-1.
\]

Since \(R^2+S^2\alpha^6=0\), the functions

\[
V=\alpha^2D/C,\qquad U=\beta/C
\]

satisfy \(U^3+V^3+1=0\). Thus
\(\eta=dV/U^2\) is the pullback of a regular elliptic differential and is closed. This is a source of nonexact closed forms, distinct from integrating a rational function of a single parameter.

Write

\[
J_X=2CR'-3RC',\qquad J_Y=2DS'-3SD'.
\]

These are precisely the homogeneous binary Wronskians \(\{C,R\}\) and \(\{D,S\}\) on the charts \((1,r)\) and \((1,s)\). Direct differentiation gives

\[
\beta^2\eta_r=\frac{\alpha^2D J_X}{3R},\qquad
\beta^2\eta_s=-\frac{\alpha^2C J_Y}{3S},
\qquad
\alpha_r=\frac{\alpha R'}{3R},\quad
\alpha_s=-\frac{\alpha S'}{3S}.
\]

Substitute these into the three source coefficients in (2.8.3). Here \(p_1=p_2=0\), so the triple is

\[
-\frac{4i}{9}J_XJ_Y(\alpha^4,\alpha^2,1).
\]

The normalized trace in the cubic algebra \(\alpha^3=iR/S\) sends both \(\alpha^2\) and \(\alpha^4\) to zero. The displayed source and its flux are independent of the remaining choice of \(\beta\), so further normalized trace leaves them unchanged. Consequently

\[
d\,\overline{\eta\wedge\Theta}
=-\frac{4i}{9}J_XJ_Y\,
  \frac{t^4}{w^5}\,dt\wedge dr\wedge ds.
\]

Rescaling the differential by \(-9/(4i)\) gives the product source \(J_XJ_Y\) exactly. The auxiliary constant \(i\) can then be removed by normalized trace. Contact coefficients can likewise be descended after taking linear combinations whose source lies in the original field; tracing an individual contact otherwise traces its source as well. In the traced flux the moving-point denominator becomes \(t^6-\alpha^6=t^6+R^2/S^2\); clearing \(S^2\) gives \(R^2+S^2t^6\), the same two-contact denominator as in the elementary field above. This calculation explains the elliptic differential encoded by that field without asserting that arbitrary coupled sources have the same trace formula.

## 2A.2 The forty-sheet contact cover

For every squarefree binary sextic \(P\), the presentations

\[
\begin{gathered}
P=C^{3}+r^{2},       \operatorname{deg} C=2,       \operatorname{deg} r=3,
\end{gathered}
\]

modulo \(C\mapsto \zeta _{3}C\) and \(r\mapsto -r\) form a finite étale cover of degree 40. Keeping these normalizations gives degree 240. This includes quadratic forms with double roots and all affine degree-drop charts; \(C\) and \(r\) remain homogeneous binary forms throughout.

To prove the claim, let \(C_P\) be the smooth genus-two curve \(w^{2}=P\). Its canonical bundle is the pullback of \(\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^{1}}(1)\). For nonzero \(T\in \operatorname{Jac}(C_P)[3]\), the degree-two line bundle \(L=K_{C_P}\otimes T\) has exactly one section up to scalar, by Riemann–Roch and \(H^{0}(T^{-1})=0\). If \(s\) is such a section, then \(s^{3}\) belongs to \(H^{0}(K^{3})=\operatorname{Sym}^{3}H^{0}(K)\oplus kw\), so \(s^3=r+a\cdot w\).

Here \(a\ne 0\). If \(a=0\), the divisor \(3\operatorname{div}(s)\) is pulled back from \(\mathbb P^{1}\), forcing \(\operatorname{div}(s)\) to be a canonical fiber: at a branch point a pulled-back multiplicity is even, and at an unramified fiber its two multiplicities agree. A degree-two divisor with these properties is canonical, which would give \(T=0\). Normalize \(a\), and multiply the identity for \(s^{3}\) by its hyperelliptic conjugate. Since the involution sends \(T\) to \(T^{-1}\), the product \(s\iota (s)\) is a quadratic canonical section. After a harmless sign and cube-root normalization the result is \(P=C^{3}+r^{2}\).

Conversely, squarefreeness forces \(\operatorname{gcd}(C,r)=1\). The identity \((w-r)(w+r)=C^{3}\) then gives \(\operatorname{div}(w-r)=3\cdot D\) for an effective degree-two divisor \(D\), and \(\mathcal O(D)\otimes K^{-1}\) is nonzero three-torsion. It cannot be zero: a canonical fiber would contain both conjugate points, whereas \(w-r\) vanishes on only one of them; branch fibers would force a common zero of \(C\) and \(r\). Changing the sign of \(r\) interchanges \(T\) and \(-T\). These operations are inverse.

Multiplication by three on a characteristic-zero abelian surface is étale of degree \(3^{4}=81\). Removing zero and dividing by the free inversion involution gives 40 sheets. One can also check étaleness of the normalized polynomial system directly: its differential is

\[
\begin{gathered}
(\delta C,\delta r) \mapsto  3\cdot C^{2}\delta C+2\cdot r\delta r.
\end{gathered}
\]

If it vanishes, coprimality forces \(r\) to divide \(\delta C\), which has degree two; thus \(\delta C=\delta r=0\). The seven-dimensional coefficient spaces therefore have invertible differential at every presentation. This also proves the coefficientwise lifting used later.

## 2A.3 Raw Wronskians span every cubic

**Raw moment theorem.** For every squarefree \(P\), the cubics \(J=\{C,r\}\) from the contact cover span \(\operatorname{Sym}^{3}\) of the binary variables.

Here is an explicit determinant proof. Rescale one initial presentation to \(P=U^{3}-V^{2}\) and form the plane cubic \(E:z^{3}-3\cdot U\cdot z+2\cdot V=0\). It is smooth. Indeed, a singular point satisfies \(z^{2}=U\) and \(V=z^{3}\); differentiating \(P\) then gives \(dP=0\). If \(z=0, U=V=0\) already makes \(P\) nonsquarefree. Either possibility contradicts the hypothesis.

For any flex tangent \(z=\xi \), where \(\xi \) is binary linear, restriction of \(E\) to the tangent is the cube of a linear form \(\eta \):

\[
\begin{gathered}
\eta ^{3}=\xi ^{3}-3\cdot U\cdot\xi +2\cdot V.
\end{gathered}
\]

For each \(\zeta ^{3}=1\) put

\[
\begin{gathered}
C_\zeta =U-\xi ^{2}-\zeta\cdot\xi\cdot\eta -\zeta ^{2}\cdot \eta ^{2},\\
S_\zeta =\eta ^{3}+2\cdot \zeta ^{2}\cdot \eta ^{2}\cdot \xi +2\cdot \zeta\cdot\eta\cdot\xi ^{2}+\xi ^{3}-2\cdot \zeta\cdot\eta\cdot U-\xi\cdot U.
\end{gathered}
\]

Expansion gives \(C_\zeta ^{3}+3\cdot S_\zeta ^{2}/4=P\). Thus these are presentations on the same cover after scaling \(S_\zeta \) by \(\sqrt 3/2\). Their Wronskians satisfy

\[
\begin{gathered}
\{C_\zeta ,S_\zeta \}=-2\{U,V\}/3+\zeta\cdot R,\\
R=(\xi ^{2}-2\cdot U)\{U,\eta \}-\xi\cdot\eta \{U,\xi \}+2\{\xi ,\eta \}V.
\end{gathered}
\]

Both identities follow by substituting \(2\cdot V=\eta ^{3}-\xi ^{3}+3\cdot U\cdot\xi \) and collecting powers of \(\zeta \) modulo \(\zeta ^{3}-1\). In particular each flex contributes the direction \(R\) to the span of the cover's raw Wronskians.

Over an algebraic closure put \(E\) in Hesse form \(X^{3}+Y^{3}+Z^{3}-3\cdot \kappa\cdot X\cdot Y\cdot Z\) and its projection center at \(O=(a:b:1)\). The Hesse normal-form theorem says that every smooth plane cubic over an algebraically closed characteristic-zero field is projectively equivalent to such a member; see [Artebani–Dolgachev, Lemma 1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/0611590). The center is outside \(E\), and outside every flex tangent: projection along a flex tangent has ramification order three and gives a multiple branch point, contradicting squarefreeness of \(P\).

The following formulas specify a nonzero maximal determinant without any elimination. Write

\[
\begin{gathered}
e=a^{3}+b^{3}+1-3\cdot \kappa\cdot a\cdot b,\\
L=(a^{2}-\kappa\cdot b)x+(b^{2}-\kappa\cdot a)y,\\
q_{0}=3\cdot a\cdot x^{2}+3\cdot b\cdot y^{2}-3\cdot \kappa\cdot x\cdot y,       c_{0}=x^{3}+y^{3},\\
\overline{U}=L^{2}-e\cdot q_{0}/3,\\
\overline{V}=e^{2}c_{0}/2-e\cdot q_{0}L/2+L^{3}.
\end{gathered}
\]

Depressing the projection coordinate gives \(U=\overline{U}/e^{2}\) and \(V=\overline{V}/e^{3}\). For a flex \(p=(p_{0}:p_{1}:p_{2})\), let \((t_{0},t_{1},t_{2})=\nabla E(p), T=t_{0}\cdot a+t_{1}\cdot b+t_{2}\), and define

\[
\begin{gathered}
\overline{\xi }=T\cdot L-e(t_{0}\cdot x+t_{1}\cdot y),\\
\eta =(p_{1}-b\cdot p_{2})x-(p_{0}-a\cdot p_{2})y,\\
\overline{R}_p=(\overline{\xi }^{2}-2\overline{U}T^{2})\{\overline{U},\eta \}-\overline{\xi }\eta \{\overline{U},\overline{\xi }\}+2\cdot T\{\overline{\xi },\eta \}\overline{V}.
\end{gathered}
\]

This is a nonzero scalar multiple of the flex direction \(R\), after clearing the nonzero denominators \(e,T\) and normalizing \(\eta \). Let \(M\) be the coefficient matrix, in the basis \(x^3,x^2\cdot y,x\cdot y^2,y^3\), of

\[
\begin{gathered}
\{\overline{U},\overline{V}\}, \overline{R}_{(0:1:-1)}, \overline{R}_{(0:1:-\zeta )}, \overline{R}_{(1:0:-1)},\\
\zeta ^{2}+\zeta +1=0.
\end{gathered}
\]

Writing

\[
\begin{gathered}
l_{1}=a+b+\kappa ,              l_{2}=a+\zeta\cdot b+\zeta ^{2}\cdot \kappa ,       l_{3}=a+\zeta ^{2}b+\zeta \kappa ,\\
l_{4}=a\kappa +\zeta\cdot b+\zeta ^{2},           l_{5}=b\kappa +\zeta ^{2}a+\zeta ,       l_{6}=b\kappa +\zeta\cdot a+\zeta ^{2},\\
l_{7}=a\kappa +b+1,             l_{8}=a\kappa +\zeta ^{2}b+\zeta ,       l_{9}=b\kappa +a+1,
\end{gathered}
\]

coefficient expansion gives, up to the sign determined by column order,

\[
\begin{gathered}
\operatorname{det} M=8748(\zeta +2)e^{5}l_{1}\cdot l_{2}\cdot l_{3}\cdot l_{4}\cdot l_{5}\cdot l_{6}\cdot l_{7}^{4}\cdot l_{8}^{4}\cdot l_{9}^{4}.
\end{gathered}
\]

The nine \(l_{i}\) are the nine flex-tangent evaluations at \(O\) up to nonzero constants. Thus every factor is nonzero. This proves rank four in the Hesse chart. Projective changes of the plane and linear changes of the projection pencil preserve the span rank, proving the theorem for every squarefree \(P\). The displayed matrix and factorization reduce the rank claim to an explicit polynomial identity.

## 2A.4 The quintic moment theorem

**Theorem.** For every squarefree binary sextic \(P\) over an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero, the forty decompositions \(P=C^{3}+r^{2}\) give classes \(C\{C,r\}\) spanning the four-dimensional quotient \(S_{5}/\langle P_x,P_y\rangle \). Together with \(P_x,P_y\) they therefore span all binary quintics.

**Proof: residue duality.** Put \(S=k[x,y]\) and \(J=\{C,r\}\). The complete intersection \(R=S/(P_x,P_y)\) has socle degree eight. Its residue pairing identifies \(R_{5}\) with the dual of \(R_{3}=S_{3}\), both of dimension four. The polynomial identity

\[
\begin{gathered}
\begin{pmatrix}P_x\\P_y\end{pmatrix}
=\begin{pmatrix}2\cdot r_x&3\cdot C_x\\2\cdot r_y&3\cdot C_y\end{pmatrix}
\cdot\begin{pmatrix}r\\C^2\end{pmatrix},\\
\det\begin{pmatrix}2\cdot r_x&3\cdot C_x\\2\cdot r_y&3\cdot C_y\end{pmatrix}=-6\cdot J
\end{gathered}
\]

and the transformation law for complete-intersection residues give

\[
\begin{gathered}
\operatorname{Res}_{P_x,P_y}(B\cdot C\cdot J)=-\operatorname{Res}_{r,C^{2}}(B\cdot C)/6,       B\in S_{3}.
\end{gathered}
\]

For \(C=a(t-\alpha )(t-\beta )\), the right-hand functional, up to its fixed nonzero scalar, is

\[
\begin{gathered}
\ell _{C,r}(B)=[B(\alpha )r(\beta )-B(\beta )r(\alpha )]/[a(\alpha -\beta )r(\alpha )r(\beta )].
\end{gathered}
\]

Indeed, reducing the one-variable residue to the two simple roots of \(C\) gives \(\sum _{C(t)=0}B(t)/(r(t)C'(t))\). Squarefreeness of \(P\) forces \(\operatorname{gcd}(C,r)=1\), so the denominators are nonzero. At \(\alpha =\beta \) the expression has the limit \([B'(\alpha )r(\alpha )-B(\alpha )r'(\alpha )]/[a r(\alpha )^{2}]\). The homogeneous residue construction includes roots at infinity. In particular, the kernel is \(\langle r\rangle +C S_{1}\), of dimension three.

**The global divisor defined by a missing moment.** Let \(H=\{w^{2}=P(x,y)\}\) be the genus-two curve and \(A=\operatorname{Jac}(H)\). Suppose a nonzero \(B\in S_{3}\) annihilated all forty \(C\cdot J\) classes. In \(H^{0}(H,3\cdot K_H)=S_3\oplus kw\), consider on \(H\times H\) the antisymmetric section

\[
\begin{gathered}
s_B(p,q)=B(p)w(q)-B(q)w(p).
\end{gathered}
\]

It is not identically zero because \(B\) and \(w\) are independent. It vanishes on the diagonal \(\Delta \). After removing \(\Delta \) it descends to a nonzero section on \(H^{(2)}=\operatorname{Sym}^2H\), since the sign change of the diagonal factor cancels the antisymmetry.

Here is its divisor class, with all multiplicities retained. Let \(x\) be the class of \(\{p_{0}+q\}\) on \(H^{(2)}\), choosing a Weierstrass point \(p_{0}\), and let \(\delta \) denote its diagonal. The canonical bundle of \(H\) is \(\mathcal O_H(2\cdot p_{0})\). Therefore the section before division has class \(6\cdot x\), and its descended divisor has numerical class \(6\cdot x-\delta /2\). The Abel map \(a:H^{(2)}\to A, D\mapsto\mathcal O(D-K_H)\), is the blowup of the origin. Riemann–Roch gives its unique point over each nonzero class and its exceptional curve \(E=|K_H|\) over zero; the graph of the hyperelliptic involution in \(H\times H\) has self-intersection \(-2\), so \(E^{2}=-1\). The quotient canonical formula gives \(K_{H^{(2)}}=2\cdot x-\delta /2\). Since \(K_A=0\), this is \(E\). A translate \(\Theta \) of the principal polarization has strict transform \(x\), hence \(a^*\Theta=x+E\). Consequently

\[
\begin{gathered}
6\cdot x-\delta /2=4\cdot a^{*}\Theta -3\cdot E.
\end{gathered}
\]

Pushing the effective divisor of \(s_B/\Delta \) to \(A\) gives a nonzero effective divisor \(Z_B\) of numerical class \(4\Theta \). In particular, \(Z_B\cdot \Theta =8\).

For every nonzero \(T\in A[3]\), its unique divisor \(D=p+q\) with \(\mathcal O(D)=K_H\otimes T\) comes from one of our decompositions. At the roots \(\alpha ,\beta \) of \(C\) its points have \(w=r\), so \(s_B(p,q)=0\) is exactly \(\ell _{C,r}(B)=0\). At double support the divided-diagonal value is the tangent expression above: on \(C=0\), differentiating \(P=C^{3}+r^{2}\) gives \(w'=r'\). Thus \(Z_B\) contains all eighty nonzero three-torsion points, including all double-support and infinity cases. We now exclude that possibility.

**A torsion-intersection bound.** Let \(G=A[3]\), of order 81, and let \(Z\) be any effective divisor of \(\Theta \)-degree at most eight on the indecomposable principally polarized surface \(A\). Every irreducible component \(E\) has \(a=E\cdot\Theta\ge2\). For \(E^{2}>0\) this follows from the Hodge index inequality \(E^{2}\le a^{2}/2\) and the fact that \(E^{2}\) is a positive even integer. If \(E^{2}=0, E\) is a translate of an elliptic curve: normalization cannot be rational on an abelian surface, and adjunction forces arithmetic genus one. If an elliptic curve had \(\Theta \)-degree one, the quotient \(A\to A/E\) would restrict to a degree-one map from the smooth genus-two theta curve to an elliptic curve, which is impossible. Such an elliptic translate contains either zero or nine points of \(G\).

Now assume \(s=E^2>0\), put \(m=|E\cap G|\) and \(h=|\operatorname{Stab}(E)\cap G|\). The stabilizer subgroup acts freely. Passing to its étale quotient gives \(s=h(E')^2\), where \((E')^2\) is a positive even integer; hence \(h\le s/2\).

Count the \(m^2\) ordered pairs of points of \(E\cap G\) by their difference in \(G\). The \(h\) stabilizer differences each contribute \(m\); each other translate is a distinct irreducible curve and contributes at most \(s\) intersection points. Since \(m\le81\),
\[
m^2\le hm+(81-h)s\le81(h+s)
\le\frac{243}{2}s\le\frac{243}{4}a^2<64a^2.
\]
Thus \(m<8a\). An elliptic component satisfies the same bound, since it contains at most nine torsion points and \(a\ge2\).

Summing over the reduced components of an effective divisor of \(\Theta\)-degree at most eight gives fewer than 64 torsion points. Multiplicities only increase the total intersection degree, so the same bound holds for a nonreduced divisor.

Thus \(Z_B\) cannot contain eighty nonzero points of \(G\). There is no missing \(B\), and residue duality proves that the \(C\cdot J\) packet spans \(R_{5}\). ∎

## 2A.5 Completion at \(q=1\)

The two moment theorems say that raw \(J\) spans every active cubic, and that gradients together with \(C\cdot J\) span every active quintic. The fields in §2A.1 therefore supply the corresponding literal target packets. It remains a finite block-degree argument, which we give explicitly.

For a target monomial let \((d_{0},d_{1},d_{2})\) be its total degrees in the three blocks, so their sum is six. A block Euler field applies whenever one \(d_{i}=4\). All remaining profiles, up to permutation, are (5,1,0), (3,3,0), (3,2,1), (2,2,2), and (6,0,0). The first three are exactly the quintic-linear, two-cubic, and cubic-linear-quadratic packets. For (2,2,2), global \(Y\)-oddness forces the mixed quadratic to be \(X_{2}\cdot Y_{2}\), so the cubic-surface construction in Chapter 2, §2.5 serves it. For (6,0,0), the only globally odd targets lie entirely in the mixed block; their \(X_{2}\) and \(Y_{2}\) exponents are both odd, so the same doubly odd construction applies. These alternatives exhaust every monomial.

Linear target separation on the finite contact cover supplies the required combinations, and normalized trace descends the fields. Every \(q=1\) target thus has a strict certificate.

## 2A.6 Completion at \(q=2\)

The binary Jacobian ring \(k[x,y]/(P_x,P_y)\) is the complete intersection of two quintics, with Hilbert function

\[
\begin{gathered}
h=(1,2,3,4,5,4,3,2,1).
\end{gathered}
\]

This follows from the Hilbert series \((1-t^{5})^{2}/(1-t)^{2}\). The full Jacobian ring of \(F\) is the tensor product of the three block rings. First consider profiles with \(d_{0}\ge 6\) or \(d_{1}\ge 6\). Every monomial in that block factors into a binary sextic coefficient direction \(T\) and a remaining monomial. The \(q=1\) theorem, differentiated in the coefficient direction \(T\) by Chapter 2's raising identity, serves the product. If \(d_{2}\ge 7\), the same reasoning works with the mixed block's even sextic directions: multiplication of their four monomials by degrees one or two spans every binary degree-seven or degree-eight monomial. If \(d_{2}=6\) and \(d_{1}\) is odd, the required mixed character is even, so it too is a coefficient direction.

These derivatives exist pointwise at every smooth member. The contact presentations form a finite étale cover. For each target choose spanning columns with a nonzero minor at the point; their inverse coefficient matrix and the polynomial flux formulas have regular formal coefficient lifts. The doubly odd cubic fields have such lifts as well: their cubic-surface lines form a finite étale cover over the passive field, since a line has normal bundle \(\mathcal O_L(-1)\) with vanishing \(H^0,H^1\), and the line-basis determinant is nonzero. Consequently every fixed target has a local strict family in every coefficient direction used above. The raising identity requires only its first derivative and preserves denominator legality.

Of the remaining profiles, any \(d_{i}=4\) is served by block Euler. Since each \(d_{i}\le 8\) in the quotient, the only profiles not yet covered are

\[
\begin{gathered}
(5,5,2), (5,2,5), (2,5,5).
\end{gathered}
\]

Indeed, the first two degrees are at most five and the third at most six; after excluding four, the only additional possibility with third degree six has odd second degree and was already covered. The \(C\cdot J\) moment theorem spans the degree-five quotient in each of the two active blocks. The first-integral product fields of §2A.1, multiplied by every quadratic in the remaining block, therefore span exactly these three profiles.

This completes the Jacobian quotient. For completeness, a target \(A\) in the degree-12 Jacobian ideal admits a parity-correct polynomial field \(w\) with \(2\cdot w(F)=A\). Put \(B=\operatorname{div} w\) and choose a \(q=1\) field \(u\) serving \(B\). Direct expansion gives

\[
\begin{gathered}
K_{2}(F,A;w+F\cdot u)=F K_{1}(F,B;u)=0.
\end{gathered}
\]

Thus the Jacobian ideal is served too, and Euler normalization supplies a strict field with zero divergence. The contact construction therefore serves both the Jacobian quotient and the Jacobian ideal. Finite trace removes the auxiliary coefficient extensions, proving the theorem.
